name: Emeka Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI companies, employers, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary day at the firm like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and fairly new to accounting, despite having a bachelor’s degree in it. I enter invoices for accounts and make the first pass at tax returns, then Nora, our senior reviewer, catches things I still miss. I like when she explains why a number is wrong; I use an AI tool now and then once someone has shown me it works. Having to redo a file for the same missed code is the tiring part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sam works in a school canteen, and our two children have homework spread across the kitchen table. The mortgage comes out of my low junior pay and Sam’s wages, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few accounting firms nearby, so a lost week of work would make us juggle bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office that a quicker first pass is welcome, as long as we still check the figures. The tax-return queue is long enough without redoing a wrong submission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage payment already takes a big piece of my junior salary, and we have less than a month saved. Even if AI barely changes work, one lost week of pay would force a difficult talk at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep entering client invoices and ask Nora, the senior accountant who checks my files, to show me the approved shortcut before I use it. In the first year I would pack lunch four days a week and put the 20 weekly saving into our mortgage buffer if my hours stay whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the mortgage, not excited by a faster screen. I can manage the queue if the firm lets me learn one check at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that difficult talk at home sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Sam that the mortgage payment comes before weekend outings for our two children. We have already cut the easy things, which is why another shortfall scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Nora show you the shortcut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nora, the senior reviewer, would run an old return beside me and let me compare her result with the software. I use AI tools now and then, but only after a colleague has proved the steps.

I would tell colleagues the **return queue** cannot absorb careless rework.
think: Our **mortgage payment** presses on my low junior salary already.

do: Keep entering **client invoices** and ask Nora to demonstrate the approved shortcut.
Pack **four lunches weekly** and add 20 to the mortgage buffer if hours hold.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the mortgage despite little change at work.

steps.text: Keep entering client invoices while asking for approved shortcut demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say our firm should show juniors exactly which tax checks the software takes, then explain how we will still learn. Otherwise a new hire has no ladder into the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do the first pass on accounts and returns, which is exactly the writing and checking software could absorb. I expect most of my first-pass hours to fall before the senior team’s, and the mortgage cannot wait while I search among a few nearby firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask Nora to let me practise the approved tax checker on three old client files after she has used it, with paid time to compare errors. I would cancel our family cinema membership and add that 35 monthly to savings; in the first year, if my hours are cut, I would apply for a vacant payroll clerk post at the firm before looking at advertised local accounting jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the work that helps me learn is the work being moved first. My children still need school shoes every term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the payroll clerk post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Payroll means checking the pay and deductions for staff, and I already reconcile wage totals on some accounts. I would only move if there is a paid vacancy with written salary and hours at least equal to mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the cinema cancellation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children we will watch films at home for a while because we need the mortgage buffer. I would not blame a computer for a decision driven by our thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the juniors that AGI by 2028 reaches tax desks in 2028, before capable robots arrive around 2031. Our first-pass work could be gone before there is a training plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to drop most junior account and tax hours once cheaper AGI can write and check the returns. Our savings will not meet even one mortgage payment, and there are too few local vacancies to assume I can replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for written notice of any hour cuts and stop paying for the children’s weekend sports club next term. If my hours fall in the first year after 2028, I would apply for any paid payroll vacancy here with written salary and hours at least equal to my present job; if none exists, I would ask Sam, my partner, whether their extra shifts could cover the mortgage while I apply to advertised local posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and ashamed about cutting the club. I have a sequence of calls to make, but the numbers are frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sam be able to take extra shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam works at a school canteen and sometimes covers another lunch shift, but those hours are not guaranteed. I would not enter the extra pay in our budget until the school confirms the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we cannot pay for the sports club next term and will play at the public field instead. They will hear enough worry in our voices without me explaining AGI to them.

I would demand **written notice** before any hours cut.

fieldNote: His **low junior standing** leaves him directly exposed at the 2028 thinking-AI date, regardless of robots arriving later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn another part of the firm, but the tax desk still changes in 2031. Robots arriving around 2034 do not keep our screens busy until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let us build two mortgage payments in savings if our pay holds, but I still expect first-pass work to shrink. I would rather practise a familiar payroll task than gamble on an expensive private course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for paid payroll training on the firm’s system and enrol only if fees and study hours are confirmed in writing. I would save 35 a month after cutting our cinema membership, while both salaries hold; in the first year after 2031 I would take a vacant payroll post only with written pay and hours at least equal to my present job, or keep any account hours while applying nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious; I can see a path, but it depends on two wages and a real vacancy. I would not tell the children we are safe yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two mortgage payments change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would let us cover a delayed payslip without missing a payment. I would put the money in a separate account so it cannot vanish into ordinary groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager will not fund training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the manager refuses funding, I would keep doing account reviews and ask a nearby firm about a posted payroll trainee job with paid hours. I cannot use our mortgage money to buy a course on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build skills and savings, but the tax returns still change when thinking AI arrives. The 2039 robot date belongs to a different part of the economy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets my children finish school and might let us pay down more of the mortgage before the first-pass work goes. I cannot assume my junior job will still exist after 2036, even if I work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep doing accounts and ask the manager for one paid payroll shift each month so I can learn by working, if they approve it. I would put 60 a month against the mortgage principal while both salaries hold; in the first year after 2036 I would move to a vacant paid payroll role only with written salary and hours no worse than now, or keep any remaining tax hours while applying to advertised nearby jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end but less trapped today. A decade is long enough to lower our mortgage balance if work stays steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put all spare cash into the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we still need a cash reserve for a broken boiler or missed shift. I would build two monthly payments first, then make the extra principal payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them that a degree opens a door, but you need people to show you the work and pay you while you learn. I would not tell them to avoid accounting just because my job may change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my first-pass work could disappear before we can save one mortgage payment. Written notice, funded payroll training and a real paid vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what my children hear when I say a shift is gone. A missed payslip is a conversation at our kitchen table before it is a line in an office plan.

headlineQuote: A missed payslip is a conversation at our kitchen table before it is a line in an office plan.
portrait: At **43**, Emeka is a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree, still learning account and tax reviews from a senior colleague.
He and **partner Sam** have two school-age children, a mortgage, low pay and less than one month saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** after a colleague proves it, and few similar jobs are nearby.
The **2028 scenario** threatens his first-pass hours; longer runways allow conditional payroll training and a mortgage reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior tax hours before the household saves even one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, funded payroll training and an actual paid vacancy.
